It is to know your responsibility on that possession.

P11.content:
When you watch a point guard, do not look only at assists or how long they have the ball.

Ask yourself:

- When do they accelerate and when do they slow down?
- How do they get the team into the offense?
- Where do they look before receiving?
- When do they use the advance pass?
- How do they organize after transition produces no advantage?
- What do they read in the pick-and-roll?
- What do they do when the first advantage disappears?
- How do they move the defense before passing?
- When do they drive to score and when do they drive to create a pass?
- Where do they go after giving up the ball?
- How do they stay threatening without monopolizing the possession?
- How do they defend the player initiating the opponent's offense?
- What do they communicate?

Also notice how many good actions happen because they chose not to attempt something harder.

P21.content:
As a point guard, you can make the game much easier for others.

Deliver the ball while the advantage still exists, not after it has disappeared.

Recognize who has a favorable matchup.

Help teammates receive in places where they can be useful.

Do not make the team wait while you decide every possession.

After passing, keep participating.

Space.

Cut.

Relocate.

Provide a return passing lane.

Screen when the action calls for it.

Being in charge of the ball does not mean the game always has to revolve around you.

P01.content:
For a shooting guard, one of the first responsibilities is learning to be useful without needing to dominate the ball.

Move with intention.

Occupy spaces the defense has to respect.

Prepare to receive.

Take the good shots the game gives you.

Attack a defense arriving off balance.

Move the ball when the advantage belongs to someone else.

Defend on the perimeter.

You do not need to prove immediately that you can create any shot.

You need to make sure the defense cannot forget about you.

P07.content:
As a shooting guard, do not disappear from the possession when the shot goes up.

On defense, box out your matchup first and pay attention to long rebounds.

Many perimeter shots produce rebounds that come outside the lane.

You can help finish the possession and, if you secure the rebound, immediately start transition.

On offense, your responsibility depends on the team's balance.

Sometimes you should attack a long rebound.

Other times you need to protect defensive transition.

Do not confuse playing far from the rim with having no rebounding responsibility.

P11.content:
When you watch a shooting guard, do not look only at how many shots they make.

Ask yourself:

- Where do they position themselves when they do not have the ball?
- How do they prepare their feet before receiving?
- When do they stay spaced and when do they cut?
- How do they set up their defender before using a screen?
- Do they use the screener tightly?
- What do they do when the defense denies the catch?
- How do they relocate after passing?
- When do they attack a closeout?
- How many dribbles do they need to create an advantage?
- When do they shoot and when do they make the extra pass?
- How do they react to help after driving?
- How do they contribute in transition?
- How do they chase their matchup through screens?
- How do they remain a threat during a possession in which they barely touch the ball?

Pay special attention to what happens **before the catch**.

Many good shooting-guard actions are already half built when the ball reaches their hands.

P21.content:
As a shooting guard, you can make the game easier for others by forcing the defense to respect your position.

Maintain space when a drive needs room.

Cut when your defender loses sight of you.

Relocate when help leaves your area.

Make the extra pass if a second player is even more open.

Attack the closeout to create something better, not simply to recover the shot that has already disappeared.

After driving, find the open teammate if the defense collapses.

Your threat has value even if you never receive.

If your movement makes help arrive late or prevents it from appearing, you are already affecting the possession.

P01.content:
For a small forward, one of the first responsibilities is learning to contribute without needing a special action designed for you.

Occupy space well.

Run.

Cut when an opportunity appears.

Shoot when you are truly open.

Attack an unbalanced defense.

Make the simple pass.

Help on the boards.

Defend in more than one area of the court.

You do not need to prove immediately that you can create from anywhere.

You need to become a useful presence in many different possessions.

P11.content:
When you watch a small forward, do not look only at how much they score.

Ask yourself:

- Where do they position themselves when someone else has the ball?
- When do they maintain spacing and when do they cut?
- How do they react after passing?
- When do they attack a closeout?
- How many dribbles do they use to decide?
- How do they contribute in transition?
- When do they crash from the perimeter?
- How do they use off-ball screens?
- When do they screen for another player?
- How do they react to a defensive switch?
- What do they do when they catch in an intermediate position?
- How do they help from the weak side?
- What types of attackers do they defend?
- How does their defense change with the matchup?
- What second action do they make after the first?

Pay special attention to possessions where they do several useful things without dominating any of them.

That is often where the real value of a good small forward appears.

P21.content:
As a small forward, you can make the game easier by connecting actions.

Maintain space when a drive needs room.

Cut when the defense turns.

Make the extra pass.

Attack a disorganized recovery.

Screen if your movement can free someone else.

Help on the boards.

Run.

Defend where the team needs you.

After a first action, look for a second one.

Do not turn versatility into an excuse to try to solve everything.

Its value lies precisely in being able to do what the possession needs without breaking it.

P01.content:
For a power forward, the first responsibilities are often tied to actions that help the team immediately.

Screen well.

Run.

Occupy useful spaces.

Box out.

Attack the ball.

Finish simple advantages.

Pass when help arrives.

Defend near and away from the rim according to the action.

You do not need to prove immediately that you have a complete set of interior moves or perimeter shooting.

You need to make the actions that can change the most possessions from your role reliable.

P07.content:
For a power forward, rebounding is often an important responsibility.

Do not wait under the rim.

Start earlier.

When the shot goes up:

- locate your opponent;
- create contact or gain position;
- box them out;
- then attack the ball.

On defense, your work may allow someone else to secure the rebound.

That ends the possession too.

On offense, learn to distinguish a good offensive rebounding opportunity from a situation where you need to protect team balance.

Attack especially from the weak side and along clear rebounding paths.

Do not confuse activity with jumping after every ball.

Good rebounding begins with reading, position and responsibility.

P11.content:
When you watch a power forward, do not look only at points or rebounds.

Ask yourself:

- What angle do they use when screening?
- When do they roll and when do they pop?
- What do they do on the short roll?
- Where do they position themselves when someone else drives?
- How do they use the high post?
- When do they cut from the weak side?
- How do they pass from interior positions?
- When do they attack a closeout?
- How many dribbles do they need?
- How do they pursue rebounds?
- Who do they box out before jumping?
- How do they participate in help defense?
- When do they protect the rim?
- How do they recover after helping?
- What do they do immediately after setting a screen?

Pay special attention to the decisions they make after the first contact or first catch.

A good power forward often contributes a great deal in those second actions.

P21.content:
As a power forward, you can make the game much easier for others.

Set screens that actually create an advantage.

Occupy the right space afterwards.

Do not close a driving lane by remaining where you are no longer useful.

Provide a passing lane on the short roll.

Find the open teammate when help arrives.

Box out so someone else can secure the rebound.

Protect the rim when help is needed.

Make the extra pass if the advantage continues outside.

A useful power forward connects interior and perimeter play.

They do not need to finish every action they help create.

P01.content:
For a center, the first responsibilities often appear in actions that repeat constantly.

Run.

Protect the rim.

Box out.

Attack the ball.

Set legal, useful screens.

Roll with intention.

Occupy spaces that allow others to drive.

Finish simple advantages.

Pass when help arrives.

Communicate.

You do not need to prove immediately that you have a complete collection of post moves or perimeter skills.

You need to make the team trust you in possessions that are decided near the rim.

P11.content:
When you watch a center, do not follow only dunks, blocks or rebounds.

Ask yourself:

- Where do they position themselves before the shot?
- Who do they box out when the rebound begins?
- How do they protect the rim without unnecessarily abandoning position?
- What angle do they use when screening?
- What do they do immediately after the screen?
- When do they roll and when do they short roll?
- How do they create depth without receiving?
- Where do they position themselves during a drive?
- How do they seal before asking for the ball?
- What do they do when defensive help arrives?
- How do they pass from the high or low post?
- What pick-and-roll coverage do they use?
- What do they communicate to the on-ball defender?
- How do they recover after helping?
- How many possessions do they change without touching the ball?

Pay special attention to what they do **before the ball arrives**.

Interior position is often won before the catch, not after it.

P21.content:
As a center, you can make the game easier for the whole team without asking for a single possession for yourself.

Set good screens.

Create depth by running to the rim.

Do not close a driving lane by occupying space someone else needs.

Provide a passing lane when the defense helps.

Pass quickly when you draw two defenders.

Box out so a teammate can secure the rebound.

Protect the rim.

Help.

Communicate.

Re-screen if the first action creates no advantage.

A useful center does not need to finish every possession near the rim.

They need to make that area easier for their team to play in and harder for the opponent.

P03.content:
In roles that alternate organization and perimeter threat, reliability includes knowing how to change roles without requiring the possession to stop.

Sometimes you will receive to initiate.

Other times you will receive an advantage that has already been created.

And sometimes your best decision will be to pass early, relocate and become an off-ball threat again.

The value lies in recognizing what the possession needs before deciding how much of the ball you need.

P06.content:
This combination requires body control both with the ball and before receiving it.

Changing pace off the dribble is important.

So are decelerating, preparing your feet, changing direction without the ball and arriving balanced to the catch.

The advantage can begin before you touch the ball and continue after you give it up.

P08.content:
In transition, decide early what the possession needs.

If you are the best outlet, show for the ball and help organize.

If someone else is already advancing it with an advantage, run wide and turn your position into a threat.

Do not run toward the ball only because you can handle it.

The ability to alternate between handling and spacing makes this combination especially useful.

P09.content:
This combination should recognize two common ways of creating advantage with screens: an on-ball screen with the ball and an off-ball screen before receiving.

The hybrid nuance is being able to move from one read to the other without changing the quality of the decision: provoke a response as the ball handler or prepare an advantageous catch away from the ball.

P10.content:
The intersection needs to connect two groups of fundamentals:

**handle, pass and read with the ball;**

**prepare your feet, catch and threaten without it.**

Work especially on the transition between the two.

Pass and stay ready.

Catch and decide without needing several dribbles.

Attack a closeout and then find the pass.

Organize an action and immediately become a perimeter option.

The combination loses value if it only works while it has the ball.

P11.content:
When watching this combination, focus especially on changes of role within the same possession.

What happens after the pass? When does creation with the ball return? How is threat maintained while someone else organizes?

Look for smooth transitions between both functions, not two separate repertoires.

P26.content:
Across all three phases, pay attention to one specific connection: being able to create with the ball and remain a threat after giving it up.

The combination progresses when both functions support each other without demanding more possession.

P03.content:
In this intersection, being reliable means being able to participate at different moments of the possession without losing clarity.

Sometimes you will need to initiate.

Other times you will connect an advantage through a pass, cut or short attack.

And sometimes your best contribution will be occupying a useful space and allowing someone else to keep creating.

Reliability lies in changing responsibility without turning every change into a new individual possession.

P07.content:
This combination can connect rebounding and transition organization in several ways.

If you secure a defensive rebound and have a clear outlet, an early pass can start the advantage immediately.

If you can advance safely, you can also launch transition without waiting for someone else to receive first.

And if you do not secure the ball, recognize early whether you should provide an outlet or run to a useful space.

The rebound does not end at the catch.

The next decision can determine the transition.

P08.content:
In transition you can alternate between handling the first advantage and running to continue it.

If you receive early, get your eyes up before accumulating dribbles.

If someone else is already advancing the ball, you do not need to come toward it to get it back.

Run.

Create space.

Cut.

Become an option ahead of the ball.

The versatility of this combination appears when you can help organize transition both with and without the ball.

P09.content:
This intersection can take part in the action as a ball handler, an off-ball user or a screener.

Its value appears when it understands which role it occupies at each moment and can connect the first screen to a second action: receive, cut, pop, create again or screen for someone else.

P11.content:
Watch how responsibility changes within the same possession.

Notice when the player initiates, when they connect an advantage through a pass or closeout, and when they cut or maintain spacing after giving up the ball.

The hybrid key is re-entering the action without stopping the offense.

P21.content:
This combination can make it especially easy to share the court with other creators.

If someone else has an advantage, you do not need to get the ball back to participate.

You can maintain spacing.

Cut.

Screen.

Relocate.

Make the pass that connects the next action.

And if the possession needs organization again, you can take it over.

Versatility has value when it reduces dependencies, not when it increases the need to touch the ball.

P22.content:
Alternating functions also expands the information you can provide.

In some actions you will be close to the ball and can help organize.

In others you will have a better view of cuts, help, switches or weak-side actions.

Learn to communicate from the place you occupy at that moment.

Not from the position written next to your name.

P26.content:
Across your development, maintain good decisions even as the place and responsibility from which you participate change.

The combination improves when organization, passing, cutting, closeout attacks and off-ball play form one continuous game.

P03.content:
In this intersection, reliability includes understanding when the possession needs you to organize and when it needs you to facilitate someone else's action.

You can initiate.

You can screen for another creator.

You can receive afterwards and move the ball quickly.

You can occupy a space that gives a drive better options.

The combination works when you do not need to be either the beginning or the end of the action to influence it.

P07.content:
This intersection can connect the end of a defensive possession especially well with the beginning of the next one.

If you secure the rebound and a clear advantage exists, get your eyes up before automatically looking for a handoff.

An advance pass can start transition.

And if you can advance safely, you can also activate the first action without waiting for someone else to receive again.

If you do not secure the ball, recognize early whether you should provide an outlet or run to a useful position.

Rebounding and organizing are not separate actions when the next decision arrives immediately.

P08.content:
In transition you can take on very different responsibilities.

Sometimes you will need to advance the ball.

Other times, run to the rim.

Arrive as the trailer.

Set an early screen.

Pop to maintain space.

Or receive in an intermediate area and connect the next action.

Do not decide your role out of habit.

Decide it based on the advantage that already exists.

The combination is especially useful when you can move from organization to depth, screening or secondary creation without slowing transition.

P09.content:
This combination can create both before and after the screen.

It can begin as the ball handler or, after screening, become a short-roll receiver, passer, pop option, handoff hub or re-screener.

The nuance is recognizing that organization of the possession can change sides within the same action.

P10.content:
This intersection needs to connect fundamentals that are often trained separately.

Ball handling and passing.

Screening and rolling.

Catching and pivoting.

Short roll and passing.

Closeout attacks.

Footwork.

Finishing.

Open shooting when it is part of your game.

It is not enough to execute each action in isolation.

Work especially on the transitions between them:

**screen → catch → read;**

**handle → pass → re-enter the action;**

**interior catch → draw help → find another advantage.**

The ability to connect fundamentals matters more than collecting moves from two different positions.

P11.content:
Pay special attention to where the possession is organized from.

Watch what happens after a screen, a short-roll catch, high-post catch or handoff, and how creation changes hands or space without losing continuity.

P21.content:
This combination can make it especially easy to play with other creators.

You can organize one action without needing to organize the next.

You can set a screen and then become a passer.

You can receive inside and find an advantage outside.

You can occupy an interior space and leave it when a drive needs room.

You can deliver the ball through a handoff and keep playing.

The ability to create from several functions should reduce the team's dependency.

It should not create a new dependency on you.

P22.content:
Alternating between actions near the ball and more interior positions can give you different views of the same possession.

When you are high on the floor, you can help organize.

When you are involved in a screen, you can communicate the action and what follows.

When you are closer to the rim, you can see help, cuts and rotations behind other players.

Learn to use the information provided by the place you occupy at each moment.

The combination expands your responsibility to communicate, not your right to talk more than anyone else.

P26.content:
The hybrid emphasis is connecting on-ball creation with creation after screening.

Short roll, high post, handoff and interior passing should expand the contexts from which you can organize without becoming a second separate development plan.

P03.content:
In this intersection, being reliable means being able to organize without always depending on the same place or action.

Sometimes the possession will need you to advance the ball.

Other times to set a screen.

To receive inside.

To pass from the high post.

To make a second decision after a short roll.

Reliability lies in recognizing which function helps the possession most and executing it without requiring everything to pass through your hands.

P07.content:
This combination can turn a defensive rebound into the first offensive decision.

If you secure the ball, do not automatically look for a nearby handoff.

Get your eyes up.

An advance pass may be available.

A lateral outlet may be available.

You may be able to advance safely.

And it may be better to give the ball up early and run to another responsibility.

The ability to organize begins before crossing half court.

Sometimes it begins exactly when the rebound ends.

P08.content:
In transition you can help from very different functions.

You can advance the ball.

Make the first pass and run to the rim.

Arrive to set an early screen.

Create depth.

Arrive at the high post.

Or become a secondary creation option after the defense has collapsed.

Do not decide in advance that you must handle or run inside.

Read where the advantage is.

The combination is useful precisely because it can help organize transition from different roles.

P09.content:
This combination can organize the action both from the initial handle and from the catch after screening.

Short roll, high post, handoff, re-screen or a weak-side pass can turn the screener into a second source of creation.

The hybrid value lies in being able to organize the possession from both moments.

P11.content:
Watch how an organizing decision can appear before or after an interior action.

Notice the connection between rebound and first pass, screen and short roll, high post and handoff, and how an advantage is directed without needing to accumulate dribbles.

P21.content:
This combination can simplify the game for others a great deal.

You can initiate a possession and then become the screener.

You can receive inside and return the ball to a better advantage.

You can create from the high post without holding the possession.

You can run a handoff and keep playing.

You can box out, make the first pass and run to another responsibility.

Your ability to organize from different places should help the team depend less on one person or one structure.

Not depend more on you.

P22.content:
This intersection can communicate from very different perspectives.

When you are high on the floor, you can help organize the action.

When you screen, you can anticipate the coverage.

When you are near the rim, you can see cuts, help and rotations behind other players.

When the possession ends, you can help organize the outlet.

Learn to communicate according to the place you occupy at that moment.

Useful information changes with your position in the action.

P26.content:
Development in this combination should expand the contexts from which you can organize: handling, rebounding, screening, short roll, high post and handoff.

The hybrid objective is to preserve simplicity and decision quality even when the place from which you connect the possession changes.

P03.content:
In this intersection, being reliable means creating threat without being limited to one way of participating.

You can be useful by shooting.

Also by cutting.

Attacking an advantage.

Making the extra pass.

Helping on the boards.

Defending on and off the ball.

The combination gains value when the defense has to respect your perimeter threat but the team can still rely on you when no shot appears.

P07.content:
This combination can have an especially useful responsibility for rebounds that come toward the perimeter.

Do not automatically leave the possession because the shot was taken far from you.

Box out first.

Read the trajectory.

Attack a long rebound when you have the advantage.

And recognize when your responsibility is protecting defensive transition.

Perimeter threat and rebounding are not incompatible functions.

The decision depends on where you are when the shot goes up.

P09.content:
This intersection should be especially comfortable connecting off-ball screens with second actions.

Coming off a screen can lead to a shot, curl, cut, immediate attack, extra pass, relocation or even a later screen for someone else.

The hybrid advantage is that off-ball movement does not necessarily end with your own catch.

P11.content:
When watching this combination, look at what happens when the first perimeter option disappears.

Notice how a denied catch or closed shot becomes a cut, closeout attack, extra pass, relocation, defense or rebounding contribution on the next action.

P21.content:
This combination makes the game easier when perimeter threat does not require stopping the possession.

Maintain space.

Cut when appropriate.

Make the extra pass.

Attack a disorganized recovery.

Help on the boards.

Defend the next action.

If an advantage created by your movement ends up benefiting someone else, the action still has value.

Threat is a tool for the team, not an obligation for you to finish the possession.

P26.content:
The emphasis of this combination is maintaining perimeter threat even when the first option disappears.

Shooting, closeout attacks, cutting, passing and defense should expand your usefulness around a reliable base, not compete to become separate specialties.

P03.content:
In this intersection, being reliable means creating threat without depending on only one way of participating.

You can create space with your position.

You can catch ready to shoot.

You can set a useful screen.

You can roll or pop.

You can attack a short advantage.

You can move the ball when help arrives.

The combination gains value when the team can use you as a threat before, during and after a screening action.

P06.content:
This combination often requires switching between perimeter movement and screening contact.

Learn to arrive balanced in both contexts.

Moving to receive requires rhythm and control.

Screening requires a base, an angle and legal position.

Attacking a closeout requires deceleration and ball protection.

Rolling after screening requires accelerating again.

The value lies in changing tasks without losing balance or clarity.

P08.content:
In transition you can create space in several ways.

Sometimes by running wide.

Other times by arriving as the trailer.

Or by arriving ready to set an early screen and pop afterwards.

Do not automatically occupy a perimeter lane or always run to the rim.

Read which space is missing.

The combination is useful when it can provide width or join a second action without slowing transition.

P09.content:
This combination can alternate between using a screen as a perimeter threat and setting one to become a different threat afterwards.

After screening, it can pop, roll, short roll, relocate, re-screen or offer a handoff.

The defense has to choose between protecting the pop, the roll and the next action.

P11.content:
Pay special attention to what happens around screens.

Watch when perimeter threat is maintained, when the player becomes the screener, and how they decide afterwards among pop, roll, short roll, pass or second action.

P21.content:
This combination is especially easy to play with when your perimeter threat also helps create advantages for others.

Space the floor.

Screen.

Roll.

Pop when it makes sense.

Catch and move the ball.

Attack late help.

Box out.

You do not need to choose between “being a shooter” and “being a screener.”

The value lies in allowing both responsibilities to coexist without stopping the possession.

P22.content:
This intersection can participate both in perimeter actions and screening coverages.

Communicate from both.

Call off-ball screens and relocations when you are outside.

And when you take part in pick-and-roll actions, communicate coverage, switch, help and recovery.

The combination expands the contexts in which you need to share information.

It does not change the principle: useful, clear and timely information.

P26.content:
Hybrid development should connect perimeter threat with play after screening.

The combination improves when shooting, popping, rolling, short roll and passing become related answers to the same defensive reaction.

P03.content:
In this intersection, being reliable means your threat does not disappear when the space you occupy changes.

You can space the floor.

You can cut to the rim.

You can screen for someone else.

You can roll.

You can receive inside and move the ball quickly.

The combination gains value when the defense has to respect you in different areas without you turning every catch into an individual action.

P08.content:
In transition you can create threat in two very different ways.

You can run wide and stretch the defense.

Or you can run directly to the rim and create depth.

You can also move from one to the other within the same transition.

If the defense protects the rim too much, space may appear outside.

If it abandons the interior, a cut or deep catch may appear.

Do not automatically occupy the space that feels most familiar.

Occupy the one that makes the possession harder to defend.

P09.content:
This intersection can transform the same action from the perimeter all the way to the rim.

It can use a screen to receive, set one to free someone else and then roll, receive inside, pop back out, offer a handoff or connect a pass.

The hybrid nuance is that the threat changes space without disappearing.

P11.content:
Watch how the player changes space without losing threat.

Notice the transition among spacing the floor, cutting, screening, receiving inside, passing against help and returning to a useful perimeter position.

Continuity between areas is the relevant trait.

P26.content:
The hybrid emphasis is maintaining threat while moving between perimeter and interior spaces.

Shooting, cutting, screening, interior catching and passing should reinforce one another instead of developing as two independent games.

P03.content:
In this intersection, being reliable means contributing even when the possession places you in different functions.

You can maintain spacing.

Cut.

Screen.

Roll.

Attack a defensive recovery.

Help on the boards.

Help and recover.

The combination gains value when you can change responsibility without the team having to change its entire structure to accommodate you.

P07.content:
This combination can take part in rebounding from very different positions.

Sometimes you will be near the rim.

Other times you will begin on the perimeter.

The responsibility changes with your location, but the principle does not.

Locate and box out first.

Then attack the ball when appropriate.

From outside, pay attention to long rebounds and weak-side crashes.

From more interior positions, preventing your opponent from reaching the ball can be especially important even if someone else eventually secures it.

On offense, always distinguish between a good offensive rebounding opportunity and the need to protect transition balance.

P08.content:
In transition you can help by creating both depth and width.

You can run to the rim.

Run a perimeter lane.

Arrive as the trailer.

Occupy a corner.

Arrive ready to screen.

Or attack a defense that is still recovering its positions.

Do not always choose the same path.

Read where the space is and which responsibility still needs to be filled.

The combination gains value when it completes the structure of transition instead of simply running to its usual area.

P09.content:
This intersection can switch sides in screening actions quite naturally.

It can use a screen and, later in the same possession, become the screener to roll, pop, short roll, relocate or create a second action.

The combination gains value when that change of responsibility keeps the advantage alive.

P11.content:
Watch how responsibility changes according to the possession.

Notice the relationship among spacing, cutting, screening, closeout attacks, rebounding and defensive help, especially after a first action that does not end with the player.

P21.content:
This combination can simplify a possession because it can cover different responsibilities without demanding a special action.

Maintain space when needed.

Cut when an opportunity appears.

Screen to free someone else.

Roll or pop afterwards.

Attack a disorganized recovery.

Make the extra pass.

Box out.

Help and recover.

Versatility has value when it allows the possession to continue.

Not when it forces the team to constantly demonstrate all the things you can do.

P26.content:
Development in this combination should increase the ability to change space and responsibility without losing reliability.

Useful versatility appears when perimeter play, screening, passing, rebounding and interior actions connect without erasing the main strengths.

P03.content:
In this intersection, being reliable means being able to contribute when the possession takes you from the perimeter to areas near the rim and back again.

You can maintain spacing.

Cut.

Screen.

Roll.

Box out.

Finish a simple advantage.

Make a pass from inside.

Help defensively near the rim.

The combination gains value when your usefulness does not disappear as you change areas.

P07.content:
This combination can reach the rebound from very different places.

If you start outside, pay attention to long rebounds and weak-side crashes.

If you are already near the rim, boxing out first may matter more than immediately chasing the ball.

Do not decide according to the position written next to your name.

Decide according to where you are when the shot goes up.

On offense, also recognize when you can attack a second chance and when you need to protect team balance.

Changing areas means changing responsibility correctly.

P08.content:
In transition you can create advantage by providing width or depth.

You can run a perimeter lane.

Attack the rim directly.

Occupy a corner.

Arrive ready to screen.

Or run ahead of the defense to establish interior position.

Do not always choose the same route.

If depth already exists, space the floor.

If presence near the rim is missing, create it.

The combination is especially useful when it recognizes early which space it needs to occupy.

P09.content:
This intersection can use a screen from the perimeter and then become an interior presence, or begin as the screener and finish the action in another space.

Roll, cut, interior catch, pop, relocation, handoff or re-screen are ways to connect both functions.

The nuance lies in changing responsibility without breaking the possession.

P11.content:
Watch how perimeter and interior play connect within the same possession.

Notice when the player spaces, cuts, screens, receives inside, crashes the glass or helps near the rim, and how they return afterwards to a useful position.

P21.content:
This combination can solve many needs within a possession without demanding a specific action.

Space the floor when someone else drives.

Cut when the defense loses a reference.

Screen when you can free someone.

Roll and force the defense to react.

Pass when help arrives.

Box out.

Protect the rim when the action places you there.

Then return to a useful space.

Versatility is there to complete the possession.

Not to constantly demonstrate how many functions you can perform.

P26.content:
The hybrid emphasis is connecting perimeter versatility with responsibilities near the rim.

Expansion should allow you to change space, screen, pass, rebound and help with interior protection without losing clarity about the dominant role.

P03.content:
In this intersection, reliability means sustaining interior responsibilities and being able to connect the possession when the action moves toward the high post, short roll or popping spaces.

Width adds value only if screening, rebounding, finishing and interior protection remain reliable.

P04.content:
The shared progression should preserve a simple idea: first a reliable interior base; then solutions that allow you to connect from more spaces.

Short roll, high post, pop or attacking a closeout are useful expansions when they improve the reading of the same role, not when they replace responsibilities that are already established.

P09.content:
This combination shares an important responsibility as a screener, but the second action can vary a great deal.

Roll, short roll, pop, re-screen, handoff, deep catch or weak-side pass allow you to alternate depth and spacing according to the defensive response.

The hybrid nuance is not turning every screen into the same roll.

P10.content:
In this combination, interior fundamentals remain the base.

Add short-roll work, high-post play, passing after help, open shooting or closeout attacks only to connect those responsibilities more effectively with intermediate or perimeter spaces.

Expansion should make your main actions harder to defend, not less reliable.

P11.content:
Watch how interior presence is maintained without congesting the floor.

Notice what happens after screening, when roll, short roll or pop is used, how the high post is played and how rebounding and rim protection connect with the next action.

P21.content:
This intersection contributes especially when interior presence also frees space.

Screening, rolling, providing a passing lane, occupying the high post or popping when appropriate should make the team's next decision easier.

You do not need to finish the action to have improved it.

P26.content:
Development in this combination should expand solutions without weakening the interior base.

Short roll, high post, popping and passing add value when they are built on already reliable screening, rebounding, finishing and rim protection.
